  1. Q1 · General English · Comprehension & Usage

    Science has discovered that the ant does not lay up anything for winter use. He is a deceiver who does not work, except when people are looking, and only then when an observer has a green, naturalistic look and seems to be taking notes. He cannot stroll around a stump and find his way home again. This amounts to idiocy. His vaunted industry is but a vanity, since he never gets home with anything he starts with. This disposes of the last remnant of his reputation and wholly destroys his main usefulness as a moral agent. It is strange, beyond comprehension, that so manifest a humbug as the ant has been able to fool so many nations, so many ages without being found out. Which claim about the ant is central to the passage?

    1. The ant prepares diligently for winter
    2. The ant only appears industrious when observed
    3. The ant navigates stumps better than other insects
    4. The ant’s industry makes it a reliable moral model
    Show answer

    Answer: (2) The ant only appears industrious when observed

    The author’s core charge is that the ant is “a deceiver who does not work, except when people are looking” – its industry is only a show for observers. The passage denies (A) and (D) outright and never compares the ant with other insects (C).

  2. Q2 · General English · Comprehension & Usage

    Science has discovered that the ant does not lay up anything for winter use. He is a deceiver who does not work, except when people are looking, and only then when an observer has a green, naturalistic look and seems to be taking notes. He cannot stroll around a stump and find his way home again. This amounts to idiocy. His vaunted industry is but a vanity, since he never gets home with anything he starts with. This disposes of the last remnant of his reputation and wholly destroys his main usefulness as a moral agent. It is strange, beyond comprehension, that so manifest a humbug as the ant has been able to fool so many nations, so many ages without being found out. What reason does the author give for calling the ant’s industry ‘vanity’?

    1. The ant brags about its work to others
    2. The ant never returns with what it starts with
    3. The ant spends too much time grooming itself
    4. The ant refuses to help other insects
    Show answer

    Answer: (2) The ant never returns with what it starts with

    The passage says: “His vaunted industry is but a vanity, since he never gets home with anything he starts with.” The word “since” gives the reason – all that effort achieves nothing.

  3. Q3 · General English · Comprehension & Usage

    Science has discovered that the ant does not lay up anything for winter use. He is a deceiver who does not work, except when people are looking, and only then when an observer has a green, naturalistic look and seems to be taking notes. He cannot stroll around a stump and find his way home again. This amounts to idiocy. His vaunted industry is but a vanity, since he never gets home with anything he starts with. This disposes of the last remnant of his reputation and wholly destroys his main usefulness as a moral agent. It is strange, beyond comprehension, that so manifest a humbug as the ant has been able to fool so many nations, so many ages without being found out. How does the author describe the ant’s navigational ability?

    1. Highly reliable under all circumstances
    2. Capable only when following pheromone trails
    3. Unable to walk around a stump and find its way home again
    4. Skilled at returning to its nest after long foraging trips
    Show answer

    Answer: (3) Unable to walk around a stump and find its way home again

    The author says the ant “cannot stroll around a stump and find his way home again”, calling this idiocy. Pheromone trails are never mentioned, and (A) and (D) contradict the passage.

  4. Q4 · General English · Comprehension & Usage

    Science has discovered that the ant does not lay up anything for winter use. He is a deceiver who does not work, except when people are looking, and only then when an observer has a green, naturalistic look and seems to be taking notes. He cannot stroll around a stump and find his way home again. This amounts to idiocy. His vaunted industry is but a vanity, since he never gets home with anything he starts with. This disposes of the last remnant of his reputation and wholly destroys his main usefulness as a moral agent. It is strange, beyond comprehension, that so manifest a humbug as the ant has been able to fool so many nations, so many ages without being found out. What is the author’s attitude toward the ant’s reputation as a moral example?

    1. Admirative and supportive
    2. Neutral and purely observational
    3. Dismissive and critical
    4. Confused but hopeful
    Show answer

    Answer: (3) Dismissive and critical

    The author says the ant’s failings dispose “of the last remnant of his reputation” and “wholly destroys his main usefulness as a moral agent”, and calls the ant a “humbug”. That is a dismissive, critical (mock-serious) tone, not an admiring or neutral one.

  5. Q5 · General English · Comprehension & Usage

    Science has discovered that the ant does not lay up anything for winter use. He is a deceiver who does not work, except when people are looking, and only then when an observer has a green, naturalistic look and seems to be taking notes. He cannot stroll around a stump and find his way home again. This amounts to idiocy. His vaunted industry is but a vanity, since he never gets home with anything he starts with. This disposes of the last remnant of his reputation and wholly destroys his main usefulness as a moral agent. It is strange, beyond comprehension, that so manifest a humbug as the ant has been able to fool so many nations, so many ages without being found out. What astonishes the author most about the ant’s image?

    1. That the ant is so industrious in winter
    2. That the ant’s deception has persisted across nations and ages
    3. That the scientists recently discovered the ant’s hoarding habits
    4. That observers cannot tell when the ant is working
    Show answer

    Answer: (2) That the ant’s deception has persisted across nations and ages

    The closing line says it is “strange, beyond comprehension” that such a humbug “has been able to fool so many nations, so many ages without being found out” – the long-lasting deception is what astonishes him.

  6. Q6 · General English · Comprehension & Usage

    Arguably, the fundamental purpose of knowledge is to improve and enrich life. Philosophy, at times, is in danger of taking itself too seriously, or losing itself in its own footnotes, and can easily forget the reasons why we seek truth and knowledge in the first place. This is not to suggest that all knowledge must have practical applications, but merely that it pays, from time to time, to step back and reassess our motivations. Nietzsche is very perceptive on this point even if it were possible to perceive the world as it really is, such knowledge would not do us any good, for knowledge is always for a purpose (even if that purpose is difficult to define or seems to be hidden from us). It’s not enough, then, to simply study the great minds of the past, imbibe their conclusions, and rehearse their arguments; genuine philosophy involves learning to think, to engage with ideas actively and critically, as opposed to merely accepting them with passive admiration. How does the passage treat the idea that all knowledge must be practical?

    1. Strongly endorses it
    2. Strongly rejects it
    3. Conditionally accepts it with caveats
    4. Claims practicality is irrelevant
    Show answer

    Answer: (2) Strongly rejects it

    The author states plainly: “This is not to suggest that all knowledge must have practical applications” – the claim is disowned, not accepted even conditionally. He only asks us to reassess our motives now and then, so practicality is not called irrelevant either.

  7. Q7 · General English · Comprehension & Usage

    Arguably, the fundamental purpose of knowledge is to improve and enrich life. Philosophy, at times, is in danger of taking itself too seriously, or losing itself in its own footnotes, and can easily forget the reasons why we seek truth and knowledge in the first place. This is not to suggest that all knowledge must have practical applications, but merely that it pays, from time to time, to step back and reassess our motivations. Nietzsche is very perceptive on this point even if it were possible to perceive the world as it really is, such knowledge would not do us any good, for knowledge is always for a purpose (even if that purpose is difficult to define or seems to be hidden from us). It’s not enough, then, to simply study the great minds of the past, imbibe their conclusions, and rehearse their arguments; genuine philosophy involves learning to think, to engage with ideas actively and critically, as opposed to merely accepting them with passive admiration. What reflective practice does the passage recommend?

    1. Memorizing canonical texts
    2. Rehearsing famous arguments
    3. Periodically reassessing our motivations for seeking knowledge
    4. Prioritizing empirical methods over theory
    Show answer

    Answer: (3) Periodically reassessing our motivations for seeking knowledge

    The passage says “it pays, from time to time, to step back and reassess our motivations” – i.e., periodically re-examine why we seek knowledge. Merely studying past thinkers, imbibing their conclusions and rehearsing their arguments is called “not enough”.

    1. Critical engagement with ideas
    2. Passive admiration of great thinkers

Why does Nietzsche think pure reality would not do us any good?

    1. Truth is always distorted
    2. Knowledge serves a purpose, not pure objectivity
    3. Philosophy cannot reach absolute truth
    4. Practical use of knowledge is unnecessary
    Show answer

    Answer: (2) Knowledge serves a purpose, not pure objectivity

    Per the passage, even a perfect perception of the world “would not do us any good, for knowledge is always for a purpose”. Knowledge matters for the purpose it serves, not as objectivity for its own sake.

  11. Q11 · General English · Comprehension & Usage

    As the term itself suggests, computers were originally meant as a mechanical replacement of human activity. ‘Computers’ were literally people who ‘computed’—using their wits, pen and paper, or else that most ancient of reckoning tools, the abacus. However, the point isn’t that machines are better at calculating than humans, merely that they can perform such calculations faster, for longer, and with fewer errors. What’s more, those errors will result from design flaws or malfunction : thus, even the computer’s mistakes are really of human origin. As the modern computer programmer puts it : “Garbage in, garbage out”—a computer is a tool, and only as good as its designer, programmer and operator. Which claim about machines versus humans does the passage make?

    1. Machines are inherently more intelligent than humans
    2. Machines are better at creative thinking than humans
    3. Machines can calculate faster, longer, and with fewer errors than humans
    4. Machines never make mistakes
    Show answer

    Answer: (3) Machines can calculate faster, longer, and with fewer errors than humans

  16. Q16 · General English · Comprehension & Usage

    People repeat ideas to signal that they are part of the same social group. But here’s a crucial point most people miss. People also repeat bad ideas when they complain about them. Before you can criticize an idea, you have to reference that idea. You end up repeating the ideas you’re hoping people will forget—but, of course, people can’t forget them because you keep talking about them. The more you repeat a bad idea, the more likely people are to believe it. Let’s call this phenomenon Clear’s Law of Recurrence : The number of people who believe an idea is directly proportional to the number of times it has been repeated during the last year—even if the idea is false. Each time you attack a bad idea, you are feeding the very monster you are trying to destroy. As one Twitter employee wrote, “Every time you retweet or quote tweet someone, you’re angry with, it helps them. It disseminates their BS. Hell for the ideas you deplore is silence. Have the discipline to give it to them”. Your time is better spent championing good ideas than tearing down bad ones. Don’t waste time explaining why bad ideas are bad. You are simply fanning the flame of ignorance and stupidity. The best thing that can happen to a bad idea is that it is forgotten. The best thing that can happen to a good idea is that it is shared. This recalls Tyler Cowen’s quote, “Spend as little time as possible talking about how other people are wrong”. Feed the good ideas and let bad ideas die of starvation. Which behaviour does the passage identify as a common way people signal group membership?

    1. Avoiding controversial topics
    2. Repeating shared ideas
    3. Critiquing group leaders
    4. Sharing private information
    Show answer

    Answer: (2) Repeating shared ideas

    Explanation: open it in the practice app. It needs the ₹149 All-in-One Pass: one payment for every exam on the site.

  21. Q21 · General English · Comprehension & Usage

    Imagine you had a bank account that deposited ₹ 86,400 each morning. The account carries over no balance from day to day, allows you to keep no cash balance, and every evening cancels whatever part of the amount you had failed to use during the day. What would you do? Draw out every rupee each day! We all have such a bank. Its name is Time. Every morning, it credits you with 86400 seconds. Every night it writes off, as lost, whatever time you have failed to use wisely. It carries over no balance from day to day. It allows no overdraft so you can’t borrow against yourself or use more time than you have. Each day, the account starts fresh. Each night, it destroys an unused time. If you fail to use the day’s deposits, it’s your loss and you can’t appeal to get it back. There is never any borrowing time. You can’t take a loan out on your time or against someone else’s. The time you have is the time you have and that is that. Time management is yours to decide how you spend the time, just as with money you decide how you spend the money. It is never the case of us not having enough time to do things, but the case of whether we want to do them and where they fall in our priorities. What is the central metaphor used in the passage to describe time?

    1. A flowing river
    2. A bank account that deposits ₹ 86,400 each morning
    3. A ticking clock
    4. A finite resource like gold
    Show answer

    Answer: (2) A bank account that deposits ₹ 86,400 each morning

  22. Q22 · General English · Comprehension & Usage

    Imagine you had a bank account that deposited ₹ 86,400 each morning. The account carries over no balance from day to day, allows you to keep no cash balance, and every evening cancels whatever part of the amount you had failed to use during the day. What would you do? Draw out every rupee each day! We all have such a bank. Its name is Time. Every morning, it credits you with 86400 seconds. Every night it writes off, as lost, whatever time you have failed to use wisely. It carries over no balance from day to day. It allows no overdraft so you can’t borrow against yourself or use more time than you have. Each day, the account starts fresh. Each night, it destroys an unused time. If you fail to use the day’s deposits, it’s your loss and you can’t appeal to get it back. There is never any borrowing time. You can’t take a loan out on your time or against someone else’s. The time you have is the time you have and that is that. Time management is yours to decide how you spend the time, just as with money you decide how you spend the money. It is never the case of us not having enough time to do things, but the case of whether we want to do them and where they fall in our priorities. Which feature of the bank account metaphor emphasizes time’s non-renewable daily nature?

    1. It allows interest to accumulate
    2. It lets you transfer time to others
    3. It permits overdrafts
    4. It carries over no balance from day to day
    Show answer

    Answer: (4) It carries over no balance from day to day

    Explanation: open it in the practice app. It needs the ₹149 All-in-One Pass: one payment for every exam on the site.
